author: Anne R. Dick
card_summary: Anne R. Dick's memoir of her marriage to Philip K. Dick (Edwin Mellen Press, 1995; revised Tachyon Publications, 2010). Anne was Dick's third wife (1959–1965), and the book covers the Point Reyes years during which Dick wrote The Man in the High Castle, Martian Time-Slip, Dr. Bloodmoney, The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, Now Wait for Last Year, and the drafts of several others. page_summary:
Anne R. Dick's The Search for Philip K. Dick (Edwin Mellen Press, 1995; revised Tachyon Publications, 2010, ed. Jill Roberts) is the only book-length memoir of PKD by a former spouse and one of the most consequential biographical sources in the literature. Anne was Dick's third wife — they married in 1959 and divorced in 1965 — and the book covers in detail the Point Reyes years during which Dick wrote his great mid-1960s novels: The Man in the High Castle (1962, Hugo winner), Martian Time-Slip, Dr. Bloodmoney, The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, Now Wait for Last Year, Clans of the Alphane Moon, The Game-Players of Titan, and drafts of several others.

Method: Anne builds the book from her own memories, from extensive interviews she conducted with Dick's friends, lovers, neighbors, and associates from the period (many of them still accessible to her in the 1990s but not to academic biographers later), and from access to documents and material objects that did not pass through formal archival channels. The Tachyon revised edition adds material developed in the years after the 1995 first edition, including responses to subsequent biographies and to the 2011 published Exegesis.

Contributions to PKD studies: (1) the only sustained first-person witness account of Dick's domestic life during the 1959–1965 Point Reyes period, the most prolific stretch in his career; (2) eyewitness corroboration or contradiction of biographical claims for those years — Anne contests Sutin's account of the marriage's collapse, the chronology of PKD's drug use, his mental state during the breakdown, and PKD's later representation of her in interviews and fiction; (3) detailed reconstruction of PKD's working methods and writing schedule from this period — material no academic biographer can match for granularity; (4) the social network of Point Reyes friendships and tensions (the Hudner family, the Tucson neighbors, the local literary community) that shaped Dick's life beyond the literary scene; (5) original research on the Episcopalian church involvement, the firearms incident, and other contested mid-1960s episodes.

Position in the literature: The Search for PKD is read as the principal corrective to Sutin's Divine Invasions (1989) on the Point Reyes period. Where Sutin reports neutrally on Anne's testimony, Anne's own account argues specific positions. Where they diverge — and they diverge on several specific matters, including the cause of the marriage's collapse, the drug-use chronology, and the question of PKD's mental state in 1963–1965 — academic biographers (Rickman, Arnold, Peake) treat both as primary sources to be weighed rather than collapsed. The 2010 Tachyon edition is widely considered the definitive text and incorporates material developed in dialogue with subsequent scholarship.

Academic and fan reception: The book is cited across academic Dick scholarship as the indispensable counter-source to Sutin and as the most detailed account of the Point Reyes period. The fan reception has been similarly central: PKD Otaku, Total Dick-Head, and the PKDS Newsletter all treat Anne's testimony as primary. The Tachyon revised edition is the recommended reference.

Caveats: Anne is a participant rather than a scholar, and the book has the character of recovered testimony — eloquent, partial, and defensible on its own terms, but not a substitute for Sutin's wider chronological coverage. The post-1965 material is necessarily second-hand. Anne's stake in how the marriage and its aftermath are remembered is foregrounded in the text rather than concealed; readers should treat the book as testimony in the sense the title gestures at — search, not closing report.

## **ACKNOWLEDGMENTS** 

I would like to thank the Philip K. Dick Estate for making the Philip K. Dick papers available to me and for permission to quote letters, documents, and some small bits of text. 

The material in this book was collected in 1982 and 1983, and the text was written in 1984. This paperback edition of 2009 is a revision, with new material added. 

Much of the original information was from interviews, tape-recorded shortly after Phil’s death. The original tapes are in the Philip K. Dick archives. My own personal memories did not include exact quotes. The dialogue is constructed but close to the spirit of the past. 

My sources for Part I of this book, a personal memoir, were my three older daughters, Hatte, Jayne, and Tandy; Phil’s Point Reyes novels; and old friends who still lived in the area: Sue Baty, Avis Hall, Inez Storer, and (interviewed briefly at the Palace Market) Pete Stephens. Thanks to them, Joan Stevens in Arizona, and June Kresy in southern California. 

I would like to thank my oldest daughter Hatte for remembering, criticizing, and endlessly listening. Thank you, second daughter Jayne who, living next door, had to listen even more than endlessly. Thanks to third daughter Tandy for your good memories of Phil and for encouraging this project. 

Paul Williams functioned as literary executor for the PKD estate for ten years after Phil’s death. I frequently visited the archives at Glen Ellen, one hour’s drive north of Point Reyes Station.
